title: The Origins of the World's Mythologies
venue: Oxford University Press (Internet Archive lending copy, full text)
ask_addressed: Is there credible evidence for very old shared mythic motifs passed down between distant cultures (e.g. Witzel's Laurasian mythology, flood and world-parent myths, the Cosmic Hunt; Berezkin's folklore distribution)? What methods are used and what are the criticisms?
quote: The common story line thus recovered can be found in most of the mythologies of Eurasia, North Africa, Polynesia, and the Americas.
summary: Witzel's own statement of the Laurasian thesis: a shared creation-to-end story line recovered by comparing whole mythologies, which he dates to the later Palaeolithic.
limits: Single-author thesis; the comparison is qualitative and the date is inferred, not measured. Witzel is the proponent, not an independent test.

strand.what: common 'Laurasian' story line from creation to the end of the world

title: The Origins of the World's Mythologies

quote: Yuri Berezkin has collected an enormous amount of such data from the Americas, from Siberia, and by now also from the rest of the world.
summary: Witzel reports Berezkin's motif-distribution maps (and principal-component analysis) as the data type that can show regional spread of single motifs, e.g. from North and Central Asia to the Americas.
limits: A secondhand description of Berezkin's work; Berezkin's own catalogue and papers were not opened.

quote: they indicate a trend while the actual geographical origin of a trait remains unclear
summary: Witzel concedes that principal-component maps of myth distribution show trends but not the origin or route of a trait; interpretation must come from archaeology or genetics.
limits: A limit stated by the proponent himself; it is not an external criticism.

title: The Origins of the World's Mythologies
venue: Oxford University Press (Internet Archive lending copy, full text)
ask_addressed: Is there credible evidence for very old shared mythic motifs passed down between distant cultures (e.g. Witzel's Laurasian mythology, flood and world-parent myths, the Cosmic Hunt; Berezkin's folklore distribution)? What methods are used and what are the criticisms?
quote: It occurs in virtually all parts of the globe and thus is not likely to have been transmitted by late diffusion
summary: Witzel argues that the flood myth is among the oldest, widely distributed and found in places without floods, so it is not a late diffusion from one centre.
limits: Argument from distribution; he also grants that similar flood myths may arise independently in river and coastal societies. No dated route is shown.

quote: Psychic universals and diffusion fail to address the central problem dealt with in the present book
summary: Witzel's framing of the rival explanations (diffusion from a centre, Jungian archetypes, Levi-Strauss's structures, convergence) that he rejects in favour of common descent.
limits: Shows the explanatory alternatives from one side; it is the proponent's dismissal, not an assessment by their defenders.

quote: point to a date of the myth well before the first immigration into the Americas
summary: Witzel argues that the sun-moon temporary-marriage myth, found in Meso-America and Eurasia, is Late Palaeolithic and predates settlement of the Americas.
limits: Dating is by distribution and presumed common descent; no text or archaeological date for the myth itself.

title: A Cosmic Hunt in the Berber sky: a phylogenetic reconstruction of a Palaeolithic mythology
venue: Les Cahiers de l'AARS 16: 93-106 (Internet Archive copy)
ask_addressed: Is there credible evidence for very old shared mythic motifs passed down between distant cultures (e.g. Witzel's Laurasian mythology, flood and world-parent myths, the Cosmic Hunt; Berezkin's folklore distribution)? What methods are used and what are the criticisms? / What does the comparative-genetic study of oral traditions (e.g. phylogenetic studies of folktales) show, and how robust is it?
quote: The results clearly support low horizontal transmissions (borrowings), Palaeolithic diffusions and punctuated evolution.
summary: d'Huy builds phylogenetic trees of 19 Cosmic Hunt versions and claims low horizontal transmission and a Palaeolithic origin; his consistency index is 0.59 and retention index 0.71.
limits: Self-published in a small series; the same author states elsewhere in the paper that some analyses may rest on insufficient data. Tree methods assume vertical descent, which is the point at issue.

title: A Cosmic Hunt in the Berber sky: a phylogenetic reconstruction of a Palaeolithic mythology
venue: Les Cahiers de l'AARS 16: 93-106 (Internet Archive copy)
ask_addressed: Is there credible evidence for very old shared mythic motifs passed down between distant cultures (e.g. Witzel's Laurasian mythology, flood and world-parent myths, the Cosmic Hunt; Berezkin's folklore distribution)? What methods are used and what are the criticisms?
quote: This motif is peculiar to Northern and Central Eurasia and to the Americas
summary: d'Huy restates, citing Berezkin 2005, that the Cosmic Hunt is attested in Northern and Central Eurasia and the Americas, with the three handle stars as hunters and the dipper as an animal.
limits: A summary of Berezkin's distribution by a second author; Berezkin's article was not opened.

title: A Cosmic Hunt in the Berber sky: a phylogenetic reconstruction of a Palaeolithic mythology
venue: Les Cahiers de l'AARS 16: 93-106 (Internet Archive copy)
ask_addressed: What does the comparative-genetic study of oral traditions (e.g. phylogenetic studies of folktales) show, and how robust is it?
quote: the results obtained with the modified data could be less reliable because there may be not a sufficient amount of data analysed
summary: In the author's own robustness check, altered data moved some versions (Tuareg with Greek, Ojibwa with Iroquoian) and the author concedes lower reliability, flagging a data-size weakness.
limits: An internal caveat by the proponent, not an independent reanalysis.

title: A Cosmic Hunt in the Berber sky: a phylogenetic reconstruction of a Palaeolithic mythology
venue: Les Cahiers de l'AARS 16: 93-106 (Internet Archive copy)
ask_addressed: What does the comparative-genetic study of oral traditions (e.g. phylogenetic studies of folktales) show, and how robust is it?
quote: These new clusters could be explained by borrowings between neighboring people
summary: In d'Huy's own tests, clusters that cut across his tree (a Tuareg version grouped with Greek ones) are attributed to borrowing, which is the horizontal transmission that tree models rely on being low.
limits: Shows by example that borrowing can mimic or break the tree signal; it is the proponent's own admission, not an external critique.
